reconcile.connective: Commentators resolve the tension by distinguishing two offers: the drugged potion Jesus refused before death, and the plain sour wine he received in his thirst at the end.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, who catalogued the passage, presses it as a flat contradiction: John has Jesus receive the vinegar and then die, where Mark and Matthew have him refuse the offered drink.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible ("Did Jesus drink on the cross?")
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), contradiction "Did Jesus drink on the cross?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: This vinegar must not be confounded with the vinegar and gall mentioned Mat 27:34, and Mar 15:23. That, being a stupifying potion, intended to alleviate his pain, he refused to drink; but of this he took a little, and then expired, Joh 19:30.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke names all three cited passages and resolves the exact tension: the drugged drink (Matt/Mark) was refused, the later plain vinegar (John) was taken — two distinct offers, not one.

excerpts.excerpt_text: They had given him vinegar to drink before they crucified him (Mat 27:34), but the prophecy was not exactly fulfilled in that, because that was not in his thirst; therefore now he said, I thirst, and called for it again: then he would not drink, but now he received it
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry distinguishes the two occasions explicitly — the earlier offer Jesus 'would not drink,' the later one in his thirst 'he received it' — the core two-drinks harmonization. (Block-anchored note.)

excerpts.excerpt_text: was different from what the soldiers gave him, which was vinegar mixed with gall … but he received it not; nor would he so much as taste of it, as he did of the other
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill marks the wine-and-myrrh (refused) as a different drink from the vinegar Jesus did taste 'of the other,' carrying the same two-drinks distinction from the Markan side.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this passage directly, distinguishing the drugged drink Jesus refused from the later undrugged drink he accepted.
